growth_story.headline: Zambia's copper-fuelled climb of 1999–2012 has stalled: income per person is at a record high, but only back to where it stood in 1965.
growth_story.arc: Zambia's income per person reached its highest level on record in 2025, but only just: it is about where it first stood in 1965, after a long fall and a slow climb back. From 1990 to 1998 it shrank by 1.5 percent a year, as copper prices collapsed, droughts hit and the loss-making state mining company, ZCCM, dug less and less copper. From 1999 to 2012 it grew by 3.5 percent a year: the mines were sold to private owners in 2000 and copper prices rose through the 2000s. Since 2013 growth has slowed to 0.6 percent a year, and to 0.5 over the last decade against 3.4 in the decade before, as copper prices fell and heavy borrowing for big building projects ended in arrears and a default in 2020, a year when income per person fell by 5.6 percent. A drought in 2024 cut farm output and electricity, and income per person rose by only 0.9 percent in both 2024 and 2025.

threads.title: Copper sets the pace
threads.text: Copper and other minerals make up most of what Zambia sells abroad, so the economy's fortunes rise and fall with copper. Copper mining needs much capital but employs few people and has weak links to the rest of the economy, so its gains spread thinly.

threads.title: State mines decline, then sold
threads.text: In the 1990s the loss-making state mining company ZCCM produced less and less copper, while copper prices collapsed from 1995 and droughts hit. ZCCM was privatized in March 2000, at the start of the faster era.

threads.title: Borrowing, default and restructuring
threads.text: As copper prices rose in the 2000s, the government borrowed heavily abroad for large building projects. When copper prices fell and revenues shrank, it fell behind on payments and in 2020 defaulted on a bond. A long restructuring has since cut the debt, though the World Bank still rates the risk of distress as high.

threads.title: Drought, dams and power cuts
threads.text: Bad weather threatens both farm output and hydroelectric power, so a poor rainy season hits food and electricity together. The 2024 drought cut farm output and brought electricity shortages that hit economic activity widely.

growth_story.tension: The World Bank calls recent growth robust, driven by foreign investment in mining, higher copper exports and gains in farming and electricity, yet in the data income per person rose by only 0.9 percent in 2025. And the record level of income per person reached in 2025 is about the same as in 1965, so the record says more about recovery than about new ground.
